newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Airlines seen making major changes.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Airlines seen making major changes.

text.p: Struggling Canadian Airlines International, facing an onslaught of tough domestic competition from upstart discount carriers, appears set to announce this week a round of major moves to help stem a steady flow of red ink.

"We do have a board meeting on Friday and the board is expected to approve our third-quarter results and we may have an announcement after that, pending board approval," Canadian spokeswoman Claudia Cattaneo said on Tuesday.
CAI is the operating unit of Canadian Airlines Corp.
Cattaneo would not confirm rumors that new initiatives would include another round of employee pay cuts that could be as high as 10 percent.
"We have been looking at ways to improve our profitability and we're looking at a number of areas," she said.

The Calgary-based airline, which has struggled financially since major expansions in the 1980s, reported a second-quarter net loss of C$23.8 million or C$0.54 a share, compared with a loss of C$25.6 million or C$0.62 a share the year before.
For the full 1995 fiscal year, Canadian lost almost C$200 million.

The company said at the end of the second quarter that much of its financial pressure this year has come from lower domestic fares to compete with no-frills price-cutters Greyhound Canada Transportation Corp's Greyhound Air and WestJet Airlines, as well as skyrocketing jet fuel costs.

This summer, controversial chief executive Kevin Jenkins was replaced by chief financial officer Kevin Benson, who said after his appointment as CEO said that Canadian had two years to turn itself into a profitable company.

Officials with the company's unions said speculation over the coming moves has included reductions to the wages of the airline's 15,000 employees, deep cuts to domestic routes and moves toward offering its own no-frills service in Canada.

"I don't discount any of them and I don't count any of them at the moment because there's some very wild ones and there's some that are not so wild," said Roger Burgess-Webb, who heads Canadian's pilots union, the Canadian Airline Pilots Association. "I'm just going to see what the announcement is."
A round of restructured agreements with all Canadian's unions that began last year is designed at saving a total of C$125 million a year in staff costs.

Flight attendent members of the Canadian Union of Public Employees -- the sole remaining union to reach an agreement with Canadian -- have yet to endorse a contract and have voted to strike if a labor deal cannot be reached.
In the past few months, the airline has also moved to boost returns from its lucrative service to Asian markets and its new routes to London, made with code-share partner British Airways.
In August, Canadian cut its flights to Frankfurt and Paris to capitalize on increasing U.K. opportunities.
It also increased its service in this winter's schedule to Asia through Vancouver's expanded terminal by 21 percent.
Asia accounts for about 25 percent of the carrier's revenues and Europe 10 percent.
